language_wrapper: There are {alpha} distinct cards carrying the consecutive integers from {start} to {end}, inclusive, arranged uniformly at random from left to right. Let a_i denote the integer on the i-th card. Consider the event E that for every i = 1, 2, ..., {alpha}, the displacement a_i - i lies between {low} and {high}, inclusive. If the probability of E equals a/x in lowest terms, determine a + x.
hardness_rationale: The seed asks for the probability that every card’s value is at least its index under a simple one-sided inequality with a constant shift, which reduces to counting permutations avoiding a single triangular forbidden region (rook polynomial on a Ferrers board). Our family imposes two-sided bounded displacement constraints a_i - i in [low, high], which creates a banded Toeplitz constraint region. Counting permutations that respect both left and right displacement bounds is strictly harder: it corresponds to the permanent of a convex 0-1 Toeplitz band matrix. A closed-form is not available in general; the natural approach uses a sliding-window bitmask dynamic program (or advanced rook polynomial decompositions) that tracks used columns within a moving interval. This requires careful state management and is not amenable to simple guessing or naive inclusion-exclusion. The verifier enforces nontrivial window widths and excludes trivial probabilities, ensuring genuine difficulty.
notes: Generalization: Let n = alpha, and the cards carry consecutive integers from start to end = start + n - 1. For each position i, we constrain the displacement a_i - i to lie in [low, high], a two-sided band. Translating to columns j in {1,...,n} with a_i = start + j - 1, the allowed columns for row i form the interval [l_i, r_i] = [i + low - start + 1, i + high - start + 1] intersected with [1, n]. Because these intervals shift right by one per row, future windows never re-expose columns that have already left the window to the left, so tracking only the currently visible window suffices. Proof sketch of DP correctness: We model the problem as a bipartite graph between rows {1,...,n} and columns {1,...,n}, with edges indicating allowable placements (convex interval neighborhoods). A perfect matching is exactly a permutation respecting all bounds. For row i, the set of permissible columns is the sliding window described above. The DP state is a bitmask over that window indicating which columns among it are already used by previous rows; when progressing to row i+1, the window shifts by one and the mask is shifted right, discarding the leftmost column that permanently leaves the allowable region. Any column outside the current window cannot be selected in this row and will only become available when it enters from the right in later rows, at which point its bit appears as 0 (unused). Conversely, any previously selected column remains within subsequent windows until it slides out to the left; during that time its bit remains 1, preventing reuse. Thus the DP counts exactly all perfect matchings, i.e., all valid permutations, without omission or duplication. The total number of permutations is n!, so the probability is count/n!, reduced to lowest terms before reporting a + x. The verifier also checks for feasibility and rejects trivial instances (probabilities 0 or nearly 1) to maintain challenge.
source_question: There are 13 cards, on which the positive integers \(2,3,\cdots,14\) are written respectively. These cards are randomly arranged in a row from left to right, and the number on the \(i\)-th card is denoted as \(a_i\), where \(i = 1,2,\cdots,13\). Let the probability that \(a_i\geqslant i\) for all \(i = 1,2,\cdots,13\) be \(\frac{a}{x}\), where \(a\) and \(x\) are relatively prime positive integers. Find the value of \(a + x\).
